issues.description: Wheel speed is repeatedly reported in m/h, yielding values around 124–146 m/h for a 1 m descent, which corresponds to ~0.034–0.041 m/s and descent times of ~25–29 s. This is implausibly slow for a wheel descending a 14-degree incline and appears inconsistent with the payoff parameters labelled as speeds. If the intended unit is cm/s or another unit, the manuscript’s reported effect sizes, maximum speed, payoff function, and interpretation of optimization are unclear and potentially wrong. Unit errors materially affect replicability and interpretation of performance.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6)) ... After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to 145.7 m/h ... Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between describing the track/descent distance as 1 meter, about one meter, 92 cm between switches, and a 2-meter rail apparatus. Because speed is the primary outcome and is calculated as distance/time, the exact distance used in calculating speed is essential. These inconsistent descriptions make it unclear whether speed was based on 1 m, 0.92 m, or another distance.
issues.quote: The physical system was a wheel that traveled down a 1-meter long inclined track.

issues.description: The methods indicate that timing switches were 92 cm apart, contradicting the stated 1-meter distance used to calculate speed. This matters because speed values and payoff calculations depend directly on the distance used.
issues.quote: Two push-button switches ... were located 92 cm apart on the rails

issues.subcategory: unclear or incorrect optimization percentage calculation
issues.description: The claim that the wheels reached 71% optimization is not explained and does not follow transparently from the reported values. If optimization is relative to first-generation speed and maximum speed, (145.7-123.6)/(154-123.6) is ~73%; if relative to payoff min/max values (96 and 160), the values differ; if relative to absolute maximum speed, 145.7/154 is ~95%. The denominator and baseline are not specified, making the claim ambiguous and potentially inaccurate.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: The main performance analyses are restricted to participants’ last two trials and appear to average only non-failure wheels in figures. Excluding early trials and failures from speed analyses can bias estimates of improvement and treatment effects, especially if failures vary by generation or treatment. Failures are part of task performance and should be modeled explicitly, e.g., with hurdle/zero-inflated models or survival/failure outcomes, rather than excluded or treated inconsistently.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.description: The figure description confirms that average speed is plotted for non-failure wheels only, while failures are merely shown as bars. This conditions the main outcome on successful descent and may exaggerate performance or obscure treatment/generation differences in failure probability.
issues.quote: Coloured lines show the average speed for non-failure wheels at each trial in each treatment.

issues.description: The manuscript states that a preregistered analysis used a final model selected after comparing candidate models based on observed-data fit. If the preregistration did not specify the exact model-selection procedure, this introduces researcher degrees of freedom and weakens confirmatory claims. Bayesian credible intervals from a selected model do not account for model uncertainty.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.description: The preregistered analysis of understanding was altered after examining the data because the original model did not converge. The revised analysis aggregated across physical principles and removed terms central to the theoretical question, changing the estimand and potentially masking divergent effects on inertia versus centre-of-mass understanding. This should be treated as exploratory or justified with alternative prespecified/robust modeling approaches.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate model for bounded count score
issues.description: Understanding score is a bounded count/binomial-like variable from 10 forced-choice items, with subscales of 5 items. The authors fit linear models to scores. Linear Gaussian models may produce invalid uncertainty estimates for bounded discrete outcomes, ignore item-level difficulty/order, and do not properly model chance performance or the three-response format. A binomial/ordinal/item-response or hierarchical logistic model would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable, “Generation” as a predictor variable and “Chain’s identity” as a random effect

issues.subcategory: understanding measure confounded by prediction task format
issues.description: The understanding test measures binary/ternary comparative prediction accuracy on 10 specific wheel pairs after experience, not explicit causal understanding. Participants may answer correctly using perceptual heuristics, memory of similar configurations, implicit learning, or local associations without causal models. Conversely, causal understanding might not translate into correct predictions for the selected pairs. Thus the measure has limited construct validity for the broad claim of absent causal understanding.
issues.quote: Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.

issues.subcategory: explicit causal understanding overinterpreted from short written theory
issues.description: In the theory condition, causal models are operationalized as a <340-character sentence beginning with a fixed stem. This format may constrain expression, omit tacit or partial understanding, and encourage simplistic unidimensional statements. Conclusions that participants do not spontaneously create multidimensional causal theories may partly reflect the elicitation format rather than true absence of richer causal representations.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.description: Theory coders were taught the experimenters’ account of the wheel dynamics and coded theories as accurate only if they matched predefined inertia/centre-of-mass statements. This may miss alternative valid causal descriptions, partial mechanisms, or pragmatic advice. The coding scheme’s validity is not fully established despite good interrater reliability.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel ... and were asked to code participants’ theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass.

issues.description: The study concludes that cultural transmission/retention across generations produces optimized solutions, but there is no control condition in which individuals receive the same number of trials without social transmission or chains. Without an asocial baseline, it is difficult to separate cumulative cultural transmission from individual learning, regression toward effective designs, shared priors, or the task’s payoff structure.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain so as to simulate overlapping generations.

issues.subcategory: causal claim exceeds design for mechanism
issues.description: The manuscript attributes improvement to selective retention of beneficial changes over generations, but the design observes generational improvement under social transmission and does not directly manipulate or isolate selective retention from other processes such as individual exploration, common heuristics, experimenter implementation, incentives, or constrained parameter space. The causal mechanism is plausible but not fully identified.
issues.quote: This confirms that the retention of improvements over generations produces highly optimized solutions and need not depend on the emergence of more accurate causal models.

issues.subcategory: absence of evidence interpreted as no effect
issues.description: The statement that theory transmission has no noticeable/substantial effect relies on credible intervals that include effects large enough to be meaningful for performance and understanding. With only 14 chains per treatment, the study may be underpowered to detect moderate treatment or interaction effects. A null-effect claim requires equivalence/ROPE criteria or Bayes factors, neither reported.
issues.quote: we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.

issues.subcategory: wide credible intervals inconsistent with strong null claim
issues.description: The reported treatment credible interval for performance ranges from a 10.76 m/h disadvantage to an 18.13 m/h advantage, which spans effects comparable to much of the observed generational improvement. This uncertainty does not support a strong conclusion of no effect of theory transmission.
issues.quote: Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h

issues.description: Data collection and analyses were not blinded to condition. Because the experimenter physically positioned the weights and released the wheel, lack of blinding could introduce subtle expectancy effects or procedural differences across treatments/generations. This is especially relevant in a mechanical task where setup and release may affect descent time.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: Participants selected configurations digitally, but the experimenter manually positioned weights on the physical wheel. The manuscript does not report checks for placement accuracy, release consistency, calibration, or whether setup errors were recorded. Manual implementation introduces measurement and performance variability that may confound outcomes.
issues.quote: Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly

issues.subcategory: measurement reliability of apparatus not reported
issues.description: The primary outcome depends on automatic timing and mechanical release, yet the manuscript does not report timing precision, calibration, repeated-run reliability for identical configurations, friction variability, or how failures/back-spinning were operationally handled. Without measurement reliability information, it is difficult to assess noise and reproducibility of speed differences.
issues.quote: Once released, the time it took the wheel to descend the track was automatically recorded by the computer program.

issues.subcategory: priors and Bayesian model details missing
issues.description: The analyses are Bayesian, but the manuscript does not report priors, likelihoods, link functions, convergence diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, effective sample sizes, or model comparison criteria. These details are needed to evaluate and replicate the analyses, especially with small numbers of independent chains.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: random effects / unit of analysis ambiguity
issues.description: Participants are nested in chains and trials are nested within participants, but the analysis descriptions do not clearly specify random slopes, nesting structure, or whether chain-level dependence across generations is adequately modeled. With only 14 chains per treatment, treating many trial observations as independent or using insufficient random effects can underestimate uncertainty.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable, “Trial”, “Generation” as predictor variables and “Player’s identity” and “Chain’s identity” as random effects

issues.subcategory: ordinal generation treated as linear without justification
issues.description: Generation appears to be modeled as a linear predictor, implying constant change per generation. Cultural accumulation may be nonlinear and bounded near a maximum; indeed performance approaches a maximum. Failure to justify or test nonlinear/growth-curve alternatives may bias estimates and conclusions about rates and treatment interactions.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable, “Trial”, “Generation” as predictor variables

issues.description: The manuscript says participants were randomly assigned to conditions and chains, but does not specify the randomization procedure, allocation concealment, balancing by sex or session time, or how chain order/generation position was assigned. These details matter because session order, participant background, or experimenter learning could confound generation or treatment effects.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition of the experiment and one sex-segregated chain.

issues.description: The manuscript reports sex-segregated chains, but the discussion claims findings generalize beyond single-sex chain compositions to mixed-gender collaborative settings. No mixed-gender chains or collaborative settings were studied, and this sentence is internally inconsistent with the design.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.description: The sample consists of French university students, yet the manuscript draws broad conclusions about humans, cultural evolution, traditional technologies, and archaeological inference. Although future non-WEIRD work is mentioned, several conclusions overgeneralize from a narrow, educated, young, Western sample and a simplified laboratory task.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly selected from a database managed by Catholic University of Lille and recruited by email from various universities in Lille, France. The subjects ranged in age from 18 to 38 y (mean of 20.5, SD of 3.4).

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from simple task to complex technologies
issues.description: The experimental task is explicitly low-dimensional and artificial, yet conclusions are extended to complex technologies such as bows, houses, kayaks, and archaeological materials. A two-variable optimization task with immediate feedback and engineered payoff may not generalize to real-world high-dimensional technologies involving materials, social coordination, long timescales, and safety constraints.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.description: The discussion uses the lab findings to caution against interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities. While caution is reasonable, the inference from a short laboratory wheel task to archaeological cognition is broad and not directly tested.
issues.quote: one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities (such as reasoning, problem-solving or planning), since these abilities are not the sole driver of technological sophistication

issues.subcategory: small number of independent chains / low power
issues.description: Although there are 140 participants, the independent units for cultural transmission are chains, with only 14 chains per treatment. This limits power for treatment, generation-by-treatment, and chain-level effects. The manuscript acknowledges no formal sample size determination, making null or weak-effect claims particularly uncertain.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications

issues.description: Exploratory analyses classify inherited theories into small groups, especially the full-theory group with N=6. Conclusions about exploration and understanding patterns in these subgroups are vulnerable to sampling error and should be treated cautiously.
issues.quote: 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses presented with causal language
issues.description: The analyses of theory type, exploration, and understanding are explicitly exploratory and based on post hoc subgrouping of naturally occurring inherited theories. Yet the manuscript uses causal language such as “strongly affected” and “inheriting ... reduces/increases understanding,” which is not warranted without random assignment to theory type.
issues.quote: Furthermore, inherited theories strongly affected participant's understanding of the wheel system.

issues.description: Participants who inherited inertia, centre-of-mass, full, or irrelevant theories were not randomly assigned. Theory type is generated by previous participants and likely correlated with chain history, prior wheel performance, transmitted configurations, participant ability, and generation. Therefore differences in exploration or understanding cannot be causally attributed to inherited theory type without stronger adjustment or experimental manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants who inherited an inertia theory mainly produced compact and balanced wheels ... In contrast, participants who inherited a centre-of-mass theory produced unbalanced wheels

issues.description: The manuscript proposes that theory transmission affects understanding via canalized exploration, but the supporting analysis groups participants by observed exploration patterns. Exploration is self-selected and confounded with ability, prior configurations, inherited information, and performance feedback. This is not a valid mediation test and cannot establish the proposed mechanism.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: chance level ambiguity in three-option task
issues.description: Participants could answer Wheel 1, Wheel 2, or No difference, but the expected score for random guessers and scoring scheme are not fully described. If all items have one correct answer among three, chance is 1/3, not 1/2; if “No difference” is never correct or rarely correct, response options alter chance and interpretation. The manuscript does not specify how “No difference” was scored or item truth structure.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide in the main text the exact 10 test pairs, their physical parameter differences, predicted descent-time differences, item difficulty, whether “No difference” was ever correct, or validation of the test. These details are necessary to evaluate whether the test fairly measures both principles and has adequate sensitivity.
issues.quote: In 5 pairs, wheels varied in their moment of inertia, in the other 5, wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass (Supplementary Figure 7).

issues.description: All participants received the same understanding-test items in the same order. Order effects, fatigue, learning during the test, or strategy shifts could bias scores or subscale differences. Randomizing or counterbalancing item order would reduce this concern.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: Chains were exclusively male or female, but sex composition is not included in the reported analyses or discussed as a potential moderator/confounder. Since chains are sex-segregated and there are equal numbers of men and women overall, imbalance across treatments or chain positions could affect results if sex or related educational background correlates with performance or exploration.
issues.quote: Two treatments were run. In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.subcategory: background covariates not reported in main analyses
issues.description: Participants reported physics or engineering background only at the end, and the discussion states it had no effect in supplementary analyses. The main manuscript does not report the distribution of this background across treatments/generations/chains or how it was modeled. Prior physics knowledge could confound understanding and performance.
issues.quote: At the end of the experiment, participants indicated whether they have an academic background in physics or engineering.

issues.subcategory: incentive structure may confound causal understanding and transmission
issues.description: Participants were rewarded both for their own performance and the next participant’s first two wheels, but final participants had doubled payoffs without knowing chain length. This complex incentive structure may affect exploration/exploitation and transmission motives differently by perceived or actual generation position, and its behavioral effects are not analyzed.
issues.quote: Participants’ final payoff corresponded to the sum of the payoff of each of their wheels plus the payoff of the next participant’ first two wheels ... Final participants in chains had their last two payoffs doubled

issues.subcategory: timing of theory writing/test phase ambiguous
issues.description: The results imply theories were formulated and transmitted after participants completed their trials, but the methods state participants wrote their theory before the test phase was completed, which is ambiguous and may mean during or after testing. If the understanding test preceded theory writing, it could affect the theory; if theory writing preceded the test, it could affect measured understanding. The exact order is important.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed.

issues.subcategory: claim of no understanding improvement despite reported interaction
issues.description: The manuscript states that understanding barely changed and that theory transmission did not affect understanding, but the reported Generation x Treatment credible interval for understanding is entirely positive (0.03, 0.81). This suggests evidence for a treatment difference in change over generations, contradicting the textual conclusion unless the effect is deemed practically negligible by predefined criteria, which are not provided.
issues.quote: Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44 ... Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: The manuscript uses “95% Confidence Intervals,” “95% credible intervals,” and “95% Highest Posterior Density Interval” for Bayesian models. These are not interchangeable, and the distinction matters for interpretation. The reporting should consistently identify posterior credible intervals/HPDIs and specify how they were computed.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h

issues.description: The maximum possible speed is central to the optimization claim, but the manuscript does not explain in the main text how “about 154” was determined, whether by exhaustive empirical testing, physical simulation, or theoretical calculation, nor its uncertainty or dependence on apparatus variability.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h

issues.description: The manuscript claims the task preserves ecological validity because the wheel obeys physics rather than arbitrary rules. However, ecological validity for culturally evolving technology involves real-world materials, social learning contexts, production constraints, and use environments. A highly constrained laboratory wheel with immediate numerical feedback may still have limited ecological validity.
issues.quote: the performance of the wheel depends solely on the laws of physics, and not on arbitrary principles that could compromise the ecological validity of our results.

issues.subcategory: overly strong framing of causal understanding as unnecessary
issues.description: The title and conclusions assert that causal understanding is not necessary for improvement of culturally evolving technology. The experiment shows improvement without measured improvement in explicit test performance in this particular task, but participants used intuitions and possibly implicit causal knowledge, and some understanding was above chance. The evidence supports a narrower claim that explicit multidimensional causal understanding was not required here, not that causal understanding generally is unnecessary.
issues.quote: Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology

issues.subcategory: implicit causal intuition conflicts with no-understanding claim
issues.description: The discussion acknowledges that participants did not randomly explore and had appropriate intuitions about acceleration, yet the main framing emphasizes absence of causal understanding. This creates a conceptual tension: biased exploration may itself reflect implicit causal understanding or learned causal priors, which would weaken claims that improvement occurred without causal understanding.
issues.quote: This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.description: Participants could consult previous configurations and scores, but the manuscript does not fully specify how these were displayed, whether order/labels/trial numbers were shown, whether failure information was included, or how inherited theories were displayed relative to configurations. These details affect social learning and replicability.
issues.quote: Social information was available all along the building phase and could be consulted between any trials in both treatments.

issues.subcategory: missing data handling not fully described
issues.description: The manuscript states no data points were excluded, but failures/non-descents were limited by restricting analyses to last two trials and figure averages use non-failure wheels. It is unclear how non-descents were coded in the dataset, whether their speeds/payoffs entered analyses, and whether any mechanical/timing errors occurred. This is a missing-data/undefined-outcome problem for the primary endpoint.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment. Coloured lines show the average speed for non-failure wheels

issues.subcategory: feedback may permit optimization without cultural transmission
issues.description: Participants received immediate numerical performance feedback after each trial and could consult their own previous configurations. This strong individual learning signal may drive much of the improvement, making it difficult to attribute optimization specifically to cultural accumulation unless compared with an appropriate individual-learning baseline.
issues.quote: The wheel’s average speed and associated payoff was then automatically displayed on the participant’s screen. Participants could consult all of their previous configurations between any trials.

issues.subcategory: multiple exploratory comparisons without uncertainty control
issues.description: The exploratory subgroup analyses compare multiple theory categories, two physical principles, exploration patterns, and understanding outcomes. The manuscript presents strong qualitative conclusions but does not report full statistical models, uncertainty intervals, or adjustments/regularization for multiple comparisons. This increases risk of false-positive or overinterpreted patterns.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior
